cards.title: Run three AI creative workflows as a test
cards.summary: Test human-only, human-briefed-AI, and AI-independent creative workflows to see which produces the best-performing ad variants for your store.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much human input to put into ad creative generation for paid acquisition.
steps: Set up three parallel workflows for the same product: (1) humans write the ad concepts unaided, (2) humans brief the AI then AI produces the creative, (3) AI generates concepts and creative independently against a defined optimization target.
Give each workflow the same outcome goal (e.g., purchases or ROAS on Meta) so results are comparable.
Run the variants as actual ads and let platform data decide the winner rather than internal taste.
Note that the source cites a study (via a podcast guest) where the AI-independent workflow outperformed both human-in-the-loop models.
Apply the winning model to scale, but keep a human check on brand and legal-sensitive claims.
caveats: The study is cited second-hand and not detailed; treat the result as a prompt to test, not a proven universal rule.
The presenter's opinion that humans are the limiting factor in creative is his view, not an established benchmark.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Measure AI revenue contribution including LLM commerce
cards.summary: Track whether LLMs become a real revenue driver, defined by the source as up to 10% of revenue sourced from or occurring within LLMs for some businesses.
cards.use_when: Forecasting marketing mix, budgeting for AI-commerce readiness, or deciding whether to invest in LLM product-feed setup for your store.
steps: Add LLM/AI-assistant traffic and assisted conversions to analytics as a distinct channel.
Define 'real' contribution using the source's heuristic of up to 10% of revenue sourced from or occurring within LLMs for some businesses.
Feed clean product feed data to LLMs using the protocols referenced in the source: ACM, UCM, and data from Shopify/Google; verify current specs before implementing.
Pair this with your website's role: the presenter argues the website is diminishing in value and commerce is becoming omnipresent (LLMs, glasses, TikTok Shop, retail, Amazon).
Invest with a longer time horizon since this is a counter-cyclical bet, per the source.
caveats: The 10% figure is the presenter's forecast for 'some businesses,' not a benchmark.
Protocol names and LLM commerce interfaces change; verify current documentation.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Follow transaction toward discovery
cards.summary: Put your transactions where people already discover products, because transaction always moves to the point of discovery.
cards.use_when: Deciding which sales channels to open or prioritize (TikTok Shop, Amazon, LLM, retail).
steps: Map where your customers currently discover your product category.
List every channel where discovery happens and whether purchase is possible there today.
Reduce friction between discovery and purchase (fewer clicks, in-platform checkout, shoppable content).
Prioritize the channel with the most attention and least purchase friction.
Reassess as discovery shifts; the source frames this as omnipresent commerce, not just omnichannel.
caveats: The priority of each channel depends on your category and customer; no universal channel ranking is implied.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Fit creative format to product complexity and funnel stage
cards.summary: Match ad format to how much information a buyer needs, then place the explanation either in the ad or the landing page.
cards.use_when: Choosing between static image and video ads and deciding what the landing page must do for a specific product.
steps: For each product, write out everything a buyer needs to know to purchase (source's 3D printer example lists plastic type, size, heat, kid-safety, software).
If the product is simple and understood, a static image ad can be highly effective and the landing page carries the rest.
If the product is complex, use longer-form video to answer questions in the ad, then drop the buyer into checkout.
If you run a static image ad for a complex product, the landing page must be excellent and cover all the questions.
Design the whole funnel (ad plus landing page) to collectively answer every question the buyer has.
caveats: The presenter rejects the image-vs-video framing as a false binary; format matters only relative to the product and funnel.
No specific format is claimed as a universal winner.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Test distinctive ecommerce creative while controlling unprofitable ad spend
cards.summary: Use the source's preference for fresh creative as a testing hypothesis within contribution and inventory limits.
cards.use_when: Managing a live ad account and planning creative rotation for the next quarter.
steps: Keep a proven ecommerce creative control while testing product demonstrations, objections and customer evidence in new formats.
Set evaluation windows and acceptable acquisition cost using the store's contribution and cash constraints.
Pause or reduce spend when losses, stock shortages or misleading claims warrant it.
Compare incremental profitable sales rather than assuming novelty or continuous spend always wins.
caveats: The source's never-stop-advertising advice is an opinion, not a rule for every store.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Treat creative as a sales obligation, not art
cards.summary: Judge creative by whether it drives a business outcome, using David Ogilvy's principle that it is only creative if it sells.
cards.use_when: Evaluating creative concepts or briefing a creative team or agency for your store.
steps: When reviewing creative, ask whether it drives a measurable business outcome rather than whether you like it.
Subordinate personal artistic preference to results in creative reviews.
Set the expectation with your creative team that ad work is evaluated on sales outcomes, not aesthetics.
Use this as the tiebreaker when a concept is liked internally but not performing.
caveats: Attributed to David Ogilvy via the source; it is a principle, not a numeric benchmark.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Write good-role / bad-role documents
cards.summary: Define what a role looks like when done badly as well as well, using the good/bad software engineer format.
cards.use_when: Writing job descriptions or onboarding docs for ecommerce roles like media buyer, retention manager, or merchandiser.
steps: Write paired statements: a good media buyer does X, a bad media buyer does Y.
Cover both the aspirational behaviors and the detrimental behaviors that can come alongside them.
Print and post the document so team members can check their behavior daily.
Use the same format for any role in your store (email marketer, buyer, ops manager).
caveats: Source notes this comes from an a16z-type document (possibly Ben Horowitz); attribution is uncertain.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Map influencer types to what you actually need
cards.summary: Influencers deliver trust, distribution, or content assets, and your job is to know which you need.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer or creator spend for your store and choosing who to work with.
steps: Identify which resource you need: (1) access to a trusting audience (e.g., a doctor for a skincare brand), (2) access to distribution at scale, or (3) content assets you can run in your ad account.
Match the person to the resource; someone with a huge audience but little trust is not the same asset as someone with a small, trusted audience.
Use their name as social proof where relevant: on your deck, your PDP, or your ad creative.
Recognize the highest-value scenario is when a partner provides trust, distribution, and assets together.
Reflect on the source's point that the two greatest influences on purchase ever are a recommendation from someone you trust and price; work those into your influencer plan.
caveats: Best case (all three) is rare; budget accordingly.
No CPM or conversion benchmarks are given.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Build a media arm to drive negative CAC
cards.summary: Use owned media to offset marketing cost so acquisition can become profit-generating rather than a pure expense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in content, podcast, or media as a customer acquisition channel for your brand.
steps: Decide first which business model the media serves: if you sell products, media drives awareness and offsets the marketing line; if you sell media itself, you need far more generalized reach.
If your model is product sales, build content aimed at a narrow, high-trust audience and let sponsorship or media revenue offset your marketing costs.
Track marketing as an offsetting revenue line so acquisition cost can trend negative.
Scale media spend only relative to the revenue it can drive back to the core business.
Recognize that a niche audience can command high CPMs from sponsors whose customer value is massive (the source cites banking/fintech sponsors).
caveats: The negative-CAC and 30%+ operating margin figures come from the presenter's service agency, not an ecommerce brand; adapt, don't assume identical results.
The presenter notes that a pure media business would require generalizing and dumbing down content, so don't blindly copy a niche strategy if media is the product.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Align dashboards to financial incentives
cards.summary: If financial incentives don't match the dashboard you show people, their behavior won't match it either.
cards.use_when: Setting team metrics or performance incentives for ecommerce roles like media buying, merchandising, or retention.
steps: Identify the primary financial metric you care about (the source's example: shareholder value).
Design dashboards so the reported metrics track the same outcome you're incentivized by.
Check that employee financial incentives point the same direction as the dashboard, or behavior will diverge.
Use equity or ownership to tie long-term behavior to that outcome.
caveats: Stated as a strong belief ('incentives drive action') by the source, not as an experimental finding.
cards.source_name: The $3B E-Commerce Strategist_ The Playbook That’s Making Everyone Else Rich.docx

cards.title: Expect harder output-expectation setting from AI
cards.summary: AI raises the ceiling on possible output so fast that rightsizing team expectations becomes the hardest management problem.
cards.use_when: Setting creative volume targets or performance expectations for a marketing or ecommerce team now that AI tools are in use.
steps: Recognize the source's question: should a marketing team produce 5, 5,000, or 50,000 pieces of creative? There is no established answer.
Set expectations relative to outcomes rather than volume, since volume ceilings have shifted dramatically.
Use AI to produce a larger exploration set and let measured results, not headcount, define what's achievable.
Revisit team targets regularly, since what took 90 days can now take minutes per the source's outbound example.
caveats: The source explicitly calls misaligned expectations his hardest current problem; this is an open question, not a solved method.
